passage:
Eleven of them had squeezed into the back of a tempo to reach the Shivratri fair, shouting over a film song. Minakshi laughed when they laughed and held the bag of roasted peanuts, but nobody had asked why she'd gone quiet since her brother left for Pune. Near the jalebi stall she felt like a lamp lit in the daytime, there but not needed.

She could have slipped off to the bus stand. She had done it before, and no one had noticed. Instead she touched Bhavna's sleeve. "Come and look at bangles with me?"

Between the glass bangles she said, "I miss home even though I'm at home. It's strange." Bhavna stopped bargaining. "I'll tell the others we'll be late," she said, and then simply listened, holding a green bangle she never bought.

qa.q: How many friends squeezed into the tempo?
Why did Minakshi feel unseen among her friends?
qa.a: Nobody had asked why she had gone quiet since her brother left for Pune, so she felt like a lamp lit in the daytime, there but not needed.

qa.q: How did Minakshi's choice at the fair differ from slipping away to the bus stand?
qa.a: She told one friend something real, so she was no longer alone with it. Slipping away would have left everyone unaware.

qa.q: What might Bhavna have felt when Minakshi said this?
qa.a: Probably surprise and care. Stopping her bargaining and offering to tell the others they would be late suggests she took it seriously.

grounding: Among many friends Minakshi feels unseen and shares something real with one person instead of withdrawing.

passage:
The fest was loud, fifty of us on the lawn, and I was the one telling jokes. That's the thing nobody gets about loneliness, Parveen. You can be the centre of the circle and feel like you're watching it through glass.
For a whole semester I kept performing. Birthday plans, trips, reels, always "Urmila's so fun". Then I'd go back to my room and not want to speak to anyone. I thought about just going quiet, dropping out of the group without telling anyone.
One night after a party, walking back, it was only me and Revathi. I didn't make a joke. I said, "Can I tell you something weird? I feel really alone even with all of you." My voice cracked.
She stopped walking. She said, "Me too, sometimes." We sat on the hostel steps till two.
So that's why I'm telling you now, Parveen, me, Urmila, the loud one: try saying one true thing to one person.

qa.q: How many people were on the lawn at the fest?
How did Urmila feel while being the fun one in the group?
qa.a: Lonely and unseen, as if watching everyone through glass, and drained enough to avoid talking to anyone afterwards.

qa.q: What small step helped Urmila, and why?
qa.a: Telling one person, Revathi, one true thing instead of joking; it turned a crowd into a real connection.

qa.q: How did Revathi respond, and what might it have meant to her?
qa.a: She stopped walking and said "Me too, sometimes"; Urmila's honesty let Revathi share her own loneliness.

grounding: Shows feeling unseen among many friends and choosing to share something real with one person instead of performing or withdrawing.

passage:
Monday: At Neel's birthday dinner, twenty friends crammed into a rooftop café, Sangeeta laughed at the right moments and posted the group photo. Nobody noticed when she left before the cake. On the metro home she muted the group chat and thought, maybe I'll just fade out.
Thursday: She almost did. Instead, after class she texted Afreen, the quietest one in the group: "Chai? Just us?" At the stall behind the library, she said it plainly: "I feel invisible with everyone lately. Like I'm there but not." Afreen put her cup down. "I noticed you left early on Monday. I wasn't sure if I should ask."
The following Sunday: At the group's picnic, Sangeeta sat next to Afreen on the mat. When the crowd got loud, Afreen caught her eye and grinned. Sangeeta unmuted the chat that night. The group hadn't changed. But she wasn't alone in it anymore.

qa.a: At a rooftop café, with twenty friends crammed in.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta feel on the metro home on Monday?
qa.a: Invisible and lonely, tempted to quietly fade out of the group.

qa.q: What turned things around for Sangeeta?
qa.a: Choosing to tell one person, Afreen, how she felt over chai, rather than withdrawing silently.

qa.q: How had Afreen seen Monday's dinner?
qa.a: She noticed Sangeeta leaving early but felt unsure whether to ask, so she was glad when Sangeeta reached out.

grounding: Illustrates loneliness in a crowd of friends changing over days once one real thing is shared with one person.
